description: Coding interviews, explained like a friend would. Plus 12 practice problems.

lessons.description: What actually happens in a coding interview — and what they're scoring.

screens.body: A typical coding interview: 45 minutes, one or two problems, you code while talking. They're not testing whether you've memorized the answer — they're testing how you THINK. A perfect silent solution scores lower than a messy narrated one.
screens.heading: The 45-minute arc

screens.body: Most interviews have two parts: coding (can you solve it?) and behavioral (can we work with you?). Coding is 60-70% of the weight for junior roles. Both parts are learnable skills, not talent.
screens.heading: Two games, not one

screens.body: Junior interviews don't expect genius. They expect: you ask questions before coding, you pick a reasonable approach, you write clean-ish code, you test it, you can say the Big O. That's the whole bar.

options: Ask, approach, code, test, Big O
check.question: The junior bar is…

screens.heading: The bar is lower than you think

screens.body: Freezing is normal — it happens to everyone. The fix isn't 'be smarter', it's 'have a framework'. When you freeze, you don't need an answer — you need the next STEP. That's what the next lesson gives you.

options: A framework for the next step
check.question: When you freeze, you need…

screens.heading: Freezing is normal

screens.body: Everything in this track maps to something you already built: Big O (CPRG 304 topic), data structures (same), talking through code (Putting It All Together). You're not starting from zero — you're assembling.
screens.heading: You're not starting from zero

screens.body: Pramp.com (free mock interviews), LeetCode Easy list, 'Cracking the Coding Interview' (the classic book).
screens.heading: Go deeper

lessons.title: How coding interviews work

lessons.description: Clarify → Plan → Code → Test → Optimize. Never freeze again.

screens.body: The framework: 1) CLARIFY — restate the problem, ask about edge cases. 2) PLAN — say your approach out loud. 3) CODE — write it. 4) TEST — run through an example. 5) OPTIMIZE — name the Big O, improve if asked. Five steps, always in order.
screens.heading: The framework

screens.body: Before touching the keyboard: 'So I need to find two numbers that add to the target — can the array have duplicates? Should I return indices or values?' Two questions asked = two signals of senior thinking. Interviewers LOVE this.
screens.heading: Clarify first

screens.body: Say the plan in one sentence: 'I'll use a hashmap to store what I've seen, so each lookup is O(1).' If the plan is wrong, they correct you BEFORE you waste 20 minutes. If it's right, you just earned trust.

options: Say the plan in one sentence
check.question: Before coding:

screens.heading: Plan out loud

screens.body: Write the simple version first — brute force is fine! Get something working, then optimize. Say: 'This works in O(n²); I can see an O(n) version with a hashmap — want me to do that?' That sentence is worth more than the optimal code.
screens.heading: Working beats clever

screens.body: Walk through your code with a real example: 'With [2,7,11,15] and target 9: i=0 stores 2, i=1 sees 7, complement 2 is in the map — return [0,1].' Testing out loud proves it works AND shows your communication.

options: Trace a real example out loud
check.question: After coding:

screens.heading: Test out loud

screens.body: The talk-through framework lives in your Putting It All Together topic too. Same muscle.
screens.heading: Go deeper

lessons.title: Talk through it: the framework

lessons.description: Name the complexity in under 10 seconds.

screens.body: 'What's the time complexity?' — you must answer in under 10 seconds. The trick: count the loops. One loop over n = O(n). Nested loops = O(n²). Halving = O(log n). No loops = O(1). Say it with confidence.
screens.heading: The 10-second answer

screens.body: Single loop? O(n). Loop inside a loop? O(n²). Binary search / halving? O(log n). Sorting? O(n log n). Array index? O(1). Five patterns cover 95% of interview questions.
screens.heading: The five patterns

screens.body: Always add space complexity too: 'O(n) time, O(n) space for the hashmap.' Two numbers, ten seconds, done. Interviewers ask 'and space?' as a follow-up — beat them to it.
screens.heading: Don't forget space

screens.body: If your solution is O(n²), say so BEFORE they ask — then offer the better one: 'This is O(n²); with a hashmap I can get O(n).' Naming your own weakness shows mastery, not failure.
screens.heading: Own your complexity

screens.body: Your Big O topic (CPRG 304) has the full drills. Re-do its quiz until the answers are reflex.
screens.heading: Make it reflex

screens.body: Your Big O & Complexity Analysis topic in Learn SD.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: You wrote the drills. Use them.

lessons.title: Big O rapid-fire

lessons.description: 'I've seen this shape before' — the pattern shortcut.

screens.body: Most interview problems are remixes of ~10 patterns. 'Find two numbers that…' → hashmap. 'Sorted array, find…' → binary search or two pointers. 'Balanced/nested…' → stack. 'Duplicates…' → set. Recognize the shape, reach for the tool.

options: Recognize the shape, reach for the tool
check.question: Pattern recognition means…

screens.heading: Shapes, not memorization

screens.body: Need fast lookups? Hashmap (O(1)). Need order + nesting? Stack. Need first-come-first-served? Queue. Sorted data to search? Binary search. The data-structure picker from your course IS the interview cheat sheet.
screens.heading: The cheat sheet
screens.keyPoint: Your course notes are the cheat sheet.

screens.body: Two pointers: one at each end of a sorted array, moving inward. Sliding window: a window that grows/shrinks over data. Both turn O(n²) into O(n). You don't need to master them today — just know their names and when they appear.
screens.heading: Two bonus patterns

screens.body: When stuck: 1) Brute force out loud (shows thinking). 2) Ask 'can I trade space for time?' (hashmap hint). 3) Ask 'is the data sorted or sortable?' (two pointers hint). Three lifelines, always available.
screens.heading: Stuck? Lifelines
Drill: name the tool
screens.body: Quick drill — say the tool out loud: 'find a pair that sums to X' → hashmap. 'Kth smallest in sorted' → binary search. 'Next greater element' → stack. 'Has this appeared before' → set. Do ten of these and the pattern muscle is built.
screens.keyPoint: Say the tool out loud, ten times.

screens.body: NeetCode.io — free, visual, pattern-organized. Better than raw LeetCode for learning.
screens.heading: Go deeper

lessons.title: Pattern recognition

lessons.description: Structure → costs → edge cases. The exact skill from that classroom moment.

screens.body: 'Explain your code' has a formula: 1) STRUCTURE — 'I used a hashmap because I need O(1) lookups.' 2) COSTS — 'It's O(n) time, O(n) space.' 3) EDGE CASES — 'Empty array returns empty; duplicates handled by…'. Thirty seconds, complete answer.
screens.heading: The 30-second formula

screens.body: Don't narrate syntax — narrate DECISIONS. Not 'then I wrote a for loop' but 'then I loop once because a single pass is enough'. Decisions show thinking; syntax shows typing.
screens.heading: Decisions, not syntax

screens.body: Practice on YOUR code — open SwiftGigs, pick a function, explain it with the formula. 'This posts a task: structure is a POST to /api/tasks; cost is one network call plus a DB insert; edge cases are empty title and no internet.' Real code, real confidence.
screens.heading: Practice on your code

screens.body: Record yourself explaining (voice memo, 60 seconds). Play it back. You'll hear filler, gaps, and — quickly — improvement. Awkward for a week, then natural. This is the highest-ROI interview prep there is.
screens.heading: Record yourself
The 10-second version
screens.body: Sometimes they just want the gist: one sentence. 'It's a hashmap two-sum: one pass, O(n) time, O(n) space.' Practice compressing every solution to one sentence — if you can say it in ten seconds, you truly understand it.

options: Split, sort, merge — O(n log n)

lessons.title: Explain your code out loud

lessons.description: STAR method, and turning your real story into answers.

screens.body: Behavioral questions ('tell me about a challenge') use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result. 2 minutes, one story, end on what you learned. Prepare 3 stories; they cover 90% of questions.
screens.heading: The STAR method
screens.keyPoint: One story, 2 minutes, end on learning.

screens.body: 'Tell me about a project' → SwiftGigs or Learn SD. 'A technical challenge' → the Byte API key bug, or building the quiz engine. 'A disagreement' → the Tomi collaboration. Your real life is full of answers — you just need them rehearsed.
screens.heading: You have the stories

screens.body: 'What's your weakness?' → name a real one plus the fix: 'I used to freeze explaining code; I built a study app and a talk-through framework, and now it's a strength.' True, specific, shows growth. Never 'I'm a perfectionist.'
screens.heading: The weakness question

screens.body: 'Why should we hire you?' → 'I build and ship: two production apps this year, I learn fast, and I communicate clearly.' Short, confident, true. Then ask THEM a question — 'what does success look like in 6 months?' — it shows you're evaluating too.

options: Short, confident, true — then ask them one
check.question: 'Why hire you?'

screens.heading: Flip it
Questions to ask them
screens.body: Always ask at least one: 'What does success look like in 6 months?' 'What's the team's biggest challenge right now?' 'How do you support junior devs?' It shows you're evaluating THEM — and their answers tell you if you even want the job.

check.question: Good question to ask them:
options: What does success look like in 6 months?

screens.body: Write your 3 STAR stories down. Out loud, once each. Done.
